But, I wanted to give a real update, as it has really been a long time coming. I will eventually be going into the though processes behind the decisions I made, and why I designed it the way I did, but that's not something I particularly want to get into today.







Anyway, below is a photo of the latest test board I made, which is designed to test a few different component layouts, and I have finally come up with what are essentially the final layouts for the boards.





























Edit (because 'enter' apparently submitted my post):







This is using a basic 3d print to make each of these segments, and I have a strategy that will look far more polished in the final version. I am coming up on the final few steps to get this project completed now, and I can't even begin to tell you how much work it has been to get this far, or how excited I am to get this finished! 







I am planning to sell these once they're done, but a few modifications have been made from what would be a 100% replica of the original. I think it makes it a better product, more suited to a Supra in today's world, but it isn't quite going to be 100% authentic.







I am extremely happy with how this is turning out. I have learned an unbelievable amount in the process of making this dream of mine a reality, and I can't wait to share the finished product. I have spent literally thousands of hours working on this project to learn what I needed in order to make it happen, and to design everything that needed designing - including two ground up redesigns from the initial concept. In the final design, there are approximately 1,000 LEDs going into every one of these gauge clusters. I am very fortunate to have been able to ask for advice from a close friend who actually has experience with designing PCBs, but aside from his advice, this entire project has been a solo labor of love. 







I'm going to go learn how to make a good rendering now so I can at least show what it should look like in the next week or two, then I'll be ordering all of the parts to put together the first few.

Yes - I am doing 
most
 of the other gauges too! I am not doing a 'TEMS gauge' - the gauge on the digital dash that had the TEMS readout, and some other things - for the initial release as I don't think the amount of effort required to make that work is worth it, considering how many cars no longer have TEMS shocks at this point. I am toying with the idea of doing one in the future that will be configurable to work with any modern adjustable coilovers (and the original TEMS shocks too), but that would be dependent on how much interest I get for that sort of thing - I will likely at least do it as a one-off for my car though. For this first version, instead of a TEMS gauge I am simply adding two additional gauges. In my car, they are going to be configured to be oil pressure and oil temperature, but with the way I am going to be making these, it will actually be pretty easy to make them display any values you want.







Currently, the initial version is planned to have the following gauges: Boost Pressure, Oil Pressure, Oil Temperature, Fuel Level, what I'm calling the 'Main Gauge' (RPM, Speed, ODO/Trip - which I'm combining into one), and the PRNDL/PWR/ECON section from the original.







For a manual transmission vehicle, I am toying with the idea of replacing the PRNDL section with a gear indicator, but that will not be present on the first version.







As far as mods, this is going to be a drop in (aside from oil temp, and possibly oil pressure) replacement. So basically, you will be able to plug in the factory harness of a LHD car and get all of the data that you could originally, which is everything except speed. I am also working on implementing an encoder that will allow you to plug the speed cable directly into this dash, so you can also get speed as though you were using the factory dash. This will also allow users to configure the speed scaling in case they have different size wheel/tire combinations so you can retain an accurate speedometer.







Additionally, there will be a CANBus input - I currently only have access to a MaxxECU Race for testing purposes, but will be reaching out eventually, as I would like to cover the most common ECU brands and their CANBus specifications (Haltech, Link at a minimum). This way any information that you want to get directly from the ECU will be super easy to retrieve, and the wiring can be simplified if you're running everything from a high end ECU anyway.







Currently, I have been focusing on the LHD version, as my car is LHD. However, I have been keeping in mind RHD during the design process, and it will actually be relatively easy to produce RHD versions. All of this will bolt directly into the factory cluster mounting system, so it will be as plug and play as I can possibly make it.







One of my other goals with this was to increase the amount of customizability available. So, there will be wifi configuration available for things like changing the brightness scaling (this cluster will still automatically dim with the factory cluster dimmer) and for changing the colors as you'd like. Here's a (pretty low quality) video showing the same base board, but with different colors (Note: one of the reasons this looks way worse is that I filmed this before I found the right way to diffuse the light):

Good job on already considering the high MPH that modern builds are capable of reaching.

Yes, the RPM bands will be configurable - the scaling on the original is very nice, because each bar on the tach represents a 100rpm jump. I haven't quite gotten into how I will scale the actual tach yet (the original goes up to 8,000rpm) but I am exploring options there which won't require me to completely redesign the PCB. I might do something similar to what older Formula 1 cars did, where the first part of the gauge uses a different scale than the rest of the gauge. So if the first 10 segments represented 200rpm each, then the tachometer could easily scale to 9,000rpm. Something like that would be very easy to implement if needed.







Thanks - I also wanted to consider anyone using kilometers as well - with how much power some MK3 Supras are making these days, I could see someone potentially hitting 400kph, which would require the 7th segment in the third digit of the speedometer.







That modern retro theme is exactly what I am going for here. At this point I'm pretty much over the whole LCD screen digital dash. They're useful and flexible, but they just don't feel special to me at this point now that every car ever is starting to come with them.

For sure - out of curiosity, what would you consider a reasonable price for something like this (assuming a very high level of quality)? For something like this, a huge part of pricing is going to come down to economies of scale. For small quantities, the per part cost of PCBA is extremely high, but the setup costs can quickly amortize across a larger run. 







For initial release, I am only planning on making a single model of cluster - it will be LHD, but will be compatible with manual and automatic transmissions, though the automatic functionality may be limited to aftermarket ECUs (As far as I'm aware, the factory automatic cluster doesn't have any display for what state the transmission is in, so there's no wiring going to the cluster for that). Other than that though, for the manual version I will just be able to turn off the LEDs related to the PRNDL stuff, and you won't be able to see that section at all through the housing. I could also potentially set up the PRNDL section to be a gear indicator. The original cluster has L2DNRP, and I could make that R12345 for a five speed or 123456 with R above (in the O/D Off segment of the original) for gear indicators. Neutral would just be all lights off I suppose. I haven't quite fully decided on how I want to do that yet though.

posts.content:
The coolant gauge assembly is now complete - including the final version (still, pending fonts) of the gauge layout: 

































I am, as always, open to feedback. These boards are all but done - for all gauges. They are only pending a design review from a friend who has far more PCB design experience than I do. Pending any changes from that design review, I will be spinning up the final design for the last board (the one that will allow this all to be plug and play with the factory wiring), and getting a design review on that. 







Once that's finished, I will need to finish all of the software involved in this project, which is fairly extensive - but I have a lot more experience writing code than I do designing PCBs, so I anticipate that will go fairly quickly. 







Finally, I will be getting the enclosure designed and built - and I'm honestly pretty excited about it. At least for this first round of clusters, I am toying with the idea of making the enclosure out of some colored plastic - similar to the translucent N64 consoles from back in the day. I think that would be a really fun throwback, even if that's only something you would see before you install it. 







After that, I will be doing all of the programming, assembling, and testing of all of the clusters. 







I feel like I can finally see the light at the end of the tunnel here - I'm excited!

As long as this thing doesn't release the blue smoke here in the next hour or two, I'm going to call it good to go - there's only a couple of minor tweaks I'm going to implement, such as an under voltage cutoff, but that looks like it will be pretty easy to do, per the datasheet!
